conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers.  
I’d like to use a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short—to see how things have felt for you over the past seven days. It’s simply 10 questions we’ll talk through together; no right or wrong answers, just whatever is true for you. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise, and we can pause any time. When you’re ready, we’ll start.

First question:  
In this past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has the joy felt a bit dimmed or missing?

Yeah, I’ve still been enjoying things, actually. Like, when my little guy smiles at me or when I get to sit down with my coffee for five minutes, those moments feel really good—pretty much the same as before. I guess the joy hasn’t dimmed.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Oh, for sure—my husband and I still crack up at silly stuff, like when the baby lets out these tiny dinosaur squeaks. I’d say I laugh just as easily as I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Yeah, I still catch myself getting excited about little plans—like our weekly walk to the coffee truck or the online moms’ group on Thursdays. I look forward to those small outings pretty much the same as always.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if I fumble a diaper change or can’t get him to nap, I might think “oops,” but I don’t beat myself up about it. I usually just shrug and try something else—no dwelling or guilt.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Maybe a teensy bit—sometimes I’ll suddenly check if he’s breathing in the middle of the night, even when he’s clearly fine. It’s not every day and it’s not overwhelming, just a quick “what if?” that passes in seconds.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like panic. I get that little “check the baby” flutter, but it’s over right away—no racing heart or real fear. I’ve never felt truly scared without a reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like yesterday when he wouldn’t settle and the laundry was piling up, I felt a bit swamped. But once my partner got home and I had a shower, everything felt manageable again. It’s momentary, not all day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, sleeping’s been okay. I go down pretty quickly once the baby’s out—my head hits the pillow and I’m out. I haven’t felt so upset that it kept me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
Honestly, I haven’t felt sad or miserable. I get tired, sure, but my mood stays pretty steady—no bouts of feeling down.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had those tears. I might get a little teary-eyed when I’m super tired, but it’s not from feeling unhappy—more like exhaustion, and it passes quickly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all. I feel okay, just tired sometimes, but never anything like that.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partnered, infant at home)  
Date: ___  
Screener: Lic. MH Professional  

I. Patient-Reported Symptoms / Concerns  
- Transient, mild worry about infant safety (brief nighttime “breathing check”; no panic)  
- Occasional feeling of being momentarily “swamped” when infant fussy + chores pile; resolves with partner support  
- Denies persistent sadness, crying spells, anhedonia, guilt, sleep-mood link, or self-harm ideation  

II. Pattern Summary  
- Mood: euthymic; pleasure in daily activities intact  
- Anxiety: situational, mild, no avoidance or physiologic panic  
- Coping: uses partner support, flexible problem-solving; no signs of clinical distress or functional impairment  

III. Screening Significance  
- Score pattern suggests low likelihood of current major postpartum depression or generalized anxiety disorder.  
- No red-flag items (persistent low mood, excessive guilt, anhedonia, sleep disruption due to mood, self-harm thoughts).  
- Continue routine postpartum monitoring; educate on normal vs. escalating anxiety; return if distress intensifies, mood drops, or function declines.
